p.src: The story tells how Tripitaka and his disciples took leave of the villagers and continued westward along the road. Before they had gone thirty or forty li, they reached the borders of the Kingdom of Western Liang. From horseback, the Tang monk pointed ahead and said, “Wukong, that city is close now, and the streets are loud with people’s voices. It must be the Women’s Kingdom of Western Liang. You must all take great care, behave properly and circumspectly, and on no account indulge wanton thoughts or violate the teachings of our faith.” The three disciples heard him and solemnly obeyed his strict command.

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, they arrived at the entrance to the eastern suburb. Everyone there wore a long skirt and short jacket, with powdered face and glossy hair; old and young alike, they were all women. They were buying and selling along both sides of the street when they suddenly saw the four travelers approaching. All together they clapped their hands, laughed delightedly, composed their features into smiles, and cried, “Men have come! Men have come!” Tripitaka was so alarmed that he reined in his horse and could go no farther. In moments the street was packed, and nothing could be heard but laughter and chatter. Bajie shouted wildly, “I’m a castrated pig! I’m a castrated pig!” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, stop talking nonsense. Just show them your old face.” Bajie promptly tossed his head twice, raised his pair of palm-leaf-fan ears, twisted his lotus-seedpod snout and dangling lips, and gave a great yell, frightening the women so badly that they stumbled and scrambled away. p.src: At this, the whole crowd grew frightened and dared not come forward. Each woman clasped her hands and stooped at the waist, shaking her head and biting her fingers. Trembling with fear, they crowded along the street and beneath the roadside, all staring at the Tang monk. The Great Sage Sun also pulled an ugly face as he cleared the way; Friar Sand put on a fierce and fearsome look to keep order; and Bajie led the horse, puckering his snout and wagging his ears.

p.src: As the party went on, they saw that the houses in the marketplace stood neat and orderly and the shopfronts were imposing. There were the usual sellers of salt and rice, wine shops and teahouses; drums and horns sounded from towers where trade flourished, while curtains hung at taverns and official lodgings. As master and disciples wound through the streets, they suddenly saw a female official standing beside the road. She called loudly, “Envoys from afar, you may not enter the city gate without authorization. Please report to the posthouse and have your names entered in the register. I shall present them to Her Majesty, whereupon your travel document will be examined and you will be allowed through.” Hearing this, Tripitaka dismounted and saw a plaque above the office inscribed with the three characters “Posthouse of Welcoming Yang.” The elder said, “Wukong, what the villagers told us was true. There really is a Posthouse of Welcoming Yang.” Friar Sand laughed and said, “Second Brother, why don’t you go look into the Child-and-Mother River and see whether you cast two reflections?” Bajie said, “Don’t make fun of me. Ever since I drank that cup of water from the Abortion Spring, the child has already come out. What would I look for now?” Tripitaka turned and admonished him, “Wuneng, guard your tongue! Guard your tongue!” He then stepped forward and saluted the female official.

p.src: The female official led the way, invited them all into the posthouse, seated them in the main hall, and at once called for tea. They saw that all her attendants likewise wore their hair in three tresses and garments divided into upper and lower pieces. Even the woman serving the tea smiled at them. Presently, they finished their tea. The female official inclined herself and asked, “Where have you envoys come from?” The Pilgrim replied, “We are imperial envoys sent by the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. My master is the Tang emperor’s sworn younger brother, known as Tang Tripitaka. I am his senior disciple, Sun Wukong. These two are my junior fellow disciples, Zhu Wuneng and Sha Wujing. Counting the horse, our party numbers five. We carry an official travel document and ask that you inspect it and permit us to pass.” After writing all this down, the female official came forward, kowtowed, and said, “My lords, forgive me. I am the superintendent of the Posthouse of Welcoming Yang. Truly, I did not know that great lords from a superior realm had arrived, or I should have gone far out to meet you.” When she had finished her obeisance and risen, she immediately ordered the steward to prepare food and drink. She said, “Please sit at ease for a while, honored sirs, while I enter the city and report to our sovereign. Your travel document will be exchanged, provisions issued, and you will be sent onward to the west.” Tripitaka gladly remained seated; of him we speak no more for now.

p.src: Now the posthouse superintendent straightened her robes and headdress, went directly into the city to the Five Phoenix Tower, and told the palace gate official, “I am the superintendent of the Posthouse of Welcoming Yang and have a matter to report to Her Majesty.” The gate official reported this at once. An edict summoned the superintendent into the audience hall, where the queen asked, “What matter have you come to report?” The superintendent said, “At the posthouse, your humble servant has received Tang Tripitaka, the sworn younger brother of the emperor of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. He has three disciples named Sun Wukong, Zhu Wuneng, and Sha Wujing, making five in all with their horse, and they wish to travel to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures. I have come especially to ask Your Majesty whether they may exchange their travel document and be permitted to pass.” When the queen heard this report, her heart filled with joy. She said to her civil and military officials, “Last night I dreamed that brilliant colors shone from a golden screen and bright light spread across a jade mirror. It was an omen of today’s happy event.” The female officials thronged forward and bowed on the vermilion steps, saying, “Your Majesty, how can you tell that it foretold a happy event today?” The queen said, “This man from the Eastern Land is the sworn younger brother of the Tang emperor. Ever since primal chaos was divided and our kingdom came into being, no man has ever come here throughout all the generations of its rulers. Now, by good fortune, the Tang emperor’s brother has descended among us. Surely Heaven has bestowed him upon me. With the wealth of my whole kingdom, I would invite the imperial brother to become king while I become his queen. Joined as woman and man, we shall beget sons and grandsons and transmit the imperial line forever. How could this not be the happy event foretold for today?” All the female officials bowed and danced in praise, and not one of them was without joy.

p.src: The superintendent reported further, “Your Majesty’s proposal is an excellent plan for perpetuating the royal house through ten thousand generations. It is only that the imperial brother’s three disciples are fierce and hideously formed.” The queen asked, “What does the imperial brother look like? And in what way are his disciples fierce and ugly?” The superintendent replied, “The imperial brother is dignified in appearance and handsome in bearing. He is truly a man of the great celestial realm and a worthy figure of China in the Southern Jambu Continent. But the three disciples are savage in form, with faces like demons.” The queen said, “If that is so, why not give his disciples their provisions, exchange their travel document, and send them on to the Western Heaven, while keeping only the imperial brother here?” The officials bowed and submitted, “Your Majesty’s words are entirely fitting. We reverently receive and obey your command. But a marriage cannot be arranged without a matchmaker. As the old saying goes, ‘A marriage is matched through the red leaf, and the Old Man under the Moon binds husband and wife with a crimson cord.’” The queen said, “As you propose, appoint the grand preceptor in attendance as matchmaker and the superintendent of the Posthouse of Welcoming Yang to preside over the marriage. Let them first go to the posthouse and propose the match to the imperial brother. Once he has consented, I shall set out in state and leave the city to welcome him.” The grand preceptor and the superintendent received the decree and withdrew from court.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tripitaka and his disciples were enjoying their vegetarian meal in the posthouse hall when someone came in from outside and announced, “The grand preceptor in attendance and our own lady superintendent have arrived.” Tripitaka said, “What can the grand preceptor’s purpose be in coming here?” Bajie said, “Perhaps the queen is inviting us to court.” The Pilgrim said, “If it isn’t an invitation, it will be a marriage proposal.” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, suppose they refuse to let us pass and force me into marriage—what are we to do?” The Pilgrim replied, “Master, just agree to it. Old Sun has a way to deal with the matter.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, the two female officials arrived and bowed before the elder. The elder returned each of their bows, saying, “I am but a monk. What virtue or ability have I, that I should trouble Your Excellencies to bow before me?” When the Grand Preceptor saw the elder’s dignified and imposing appearance, she secretly rejoiced: “Our kingdom is truly blessed. This man is indeed fit to become our sovereign’s husband.” After the two officials had finished bowing, they rose and stood in attendance on either side, saying, “Your Highness, a thousand congratulations!” Tripitaka said, “I am a monk. What cause have I for congratulations?” The Grand Preceptor bowed and said, “This is the Women’s Kingdom of Western Liang, where there has never been a man. Now, by good fortune, Your Highness has descended upon us. By command of our sovereign, I have come expressly to propose a marriage.” Tripitaka said, “Blessed be! Blessed be! This poor monk came alone to your honored land, with neither son nor daughter beside him, but only three unruly disciples. I do not know for whom Your Excellency seeks this marriage.” The posthouse mistress said, “When this humble official entered court just now and reported your arrival, our sovereign was overjoyed and said that last night she had an auspicious dream, in which a golden screen shone with splendid colors and a jade mirror cast forth brilliant light. Your Highness is a man of the great central realm of China. Our sovereign wishes to offer the wealth of her entire kingdom and take Your Highness as her husband. You shall sit facing south and rule as sovereign, while our queen shall become your imperial consort. She issued a decree appointing the Grand Preceptor as matchmaker and this humble official to preside over the wedding. That is why we have come expressly to propose this marriage.” On hearing this, Tripitaka lowered his head and said nothing. The Grand Preceptor said, “When opportunity comes to a true man, he must not let it pass. Though marriages in which a man enters the woman’s household are found under heaven, it is exceedingly rare for an entire kingdom’s wealth to be entrusted to him. Please consent at once, Your Highness, so that we may return and report.” The elder became more tongue-tied than ever.

p.src: Standing nearby, Eight Rules thrust out his long, pestle-like snout and cried, “Grand Preceptor, go back and tell the sovereign this: my master is an arhat who has cultivated the Way for many years. He certainly does not covet the wealth of your whole kingdom, nor does he desire your sovereign’s beauty, fair enough to topple a realm. Quickly certify our travel documents and send him on his way west, but leave me here to become the royal son-in-law. How would that be?” Hearing this, the Grand Preceptor trembled with fear and dared not reply. The posthouse mistress said, “Though you are male, your appearance is ugly and would not please our sovereign.” Eight Rules laughed and said, “You are remarkably inflexible. As the saying goes, ‘Coarse willow makes a winnowing basket and fine willow a grain measure—who ever saw an ugly man in this world?’” Pilgrim said, “Idiot, stop talking nonsense. Let Master decide as he sees fit: let it proceed if it may, or cease if it must. Do not hold up the matchmakers in their work.”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Wukong, what do you think we should say?” Pilgrim replied, “In old Monkey’s opinion, it would be well for you to remain here. As the old saying goes, ‘A marriage across a thousand miles is drawn together by a thread.’ Where else could you find a match so perfectly suited?” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, if we remain here coveting wealth and honor, who will go to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures? Would that not betray the hopes of my sovereign, the emperor of the Great Tang?” The Grand Preceptor said, “Your Highness, this humble minister would not dare conceal the truth. Our sovereign’s decree was only that we seek Your Highness in marriage. Your three disciples are to attend the wedding banquet, receive provisions, have the travel documents certified, and then depart for the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures.” Pilgrim said, “The Grand Preceptor speaks reasonably. There is no need for us to make difficulties. We are willing to leave our master here to become your sovereign’s husband. Quickly certify our travel documents and send us on our way west. When we return with the scriptures, we can come here to pay respects to our father and mother, ask for traveling expenses, and then return to the Great Tang.” The Grand Preceptor and the posthouse mistress bowed to Pilgrim and said, “Many thanks, venerable master, for bringing this match to fruition.” Eight Rules said, “Grand Preceptor, do not merely set out dishes with your mouth. Since we have given our consent, have your sovereign first prepare a feast and let us drink a cup of betrothal wine. What do you say?” The Grand Preceptor said, “Yes, yes, certainly! We shall have the banquet set out at once.” The posthouse mistress and the Grand Preceptor, beside themselves with joy, returned to report to the queen. We shall say no more of them for now.

p.src: Now the Tang elder seized Pilgrim and cursed him: “You monkey! You have done me to death! How could you say such things—telling me to marry here while you go worship the Buddha in the Western Heaven? Even if it means my death, I would never dare do such a thing.” Pilgrim said, “Do not worry, Master. How could old Monkey not know your nature? But having come to this place and met these people, we have no choice but to turn their scheme to our own advantage.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean by turning their scheme to our advantage?” Pilgrim said, “If you stubbornly refuse her outright, she will not certify our travel documents or allow us to continue our journey. If by chance she turns malicious and cruel, orders a crowd to cut off your flesh, and makes it into scented sachets or some such thing, what good reward would there be for us? We would surely have to employ our divine powers for subduing demons and sweeping away monsters. You know how heavy our hands are and how fearsome our weapons; once we began fighting, we would kill every person in this kingdom. Though they obstruct us, they are not monsters or demons, but human beings of an entire kingdom. Moreover, you have always been a benevolent and compassionate man who harms not even a single living soul upon the road. If countless innocent people were killed, how could your heart endure it? It would truly be an evil deed.” After hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, your reasoning is excellent. But I fear that once the queen summons me inside, she will demand the rites of husband and wife. How could I consent to lose my primal yang and ruin the virtue of the Buddhist order? How could I spill my true essence and cast away the human body attained within our faith?” Pilgrim said, “Once you consent to the marriage today, she will surely come out of the city with an imperial procession to receive you with the honors due an emperor. Do not refuse her. Simply ride in her phoenix palanquin or dragon carriage, ascend the jeweled hall, and take your seat facing south. Ask the queen to bring out the imperial seal, summon us brothers to court, stamp our travel rescript, and then have the queen write and sign an endorsement before handing it over to us. Meanwhile, have a banquet prepared; it can serve at once to celebrate your union with the queen and to bid us farewell. When the banquet is over, order the procession prepared again, saying that you will escort the three of us out of the city and return afterward to be joined with the queen. Thus you will beguile the queen and her ministers into rejoicing, so that they harbor no thought of obstructing us and conceive no cruel or malicious intent. Once they have escorted us beyond the city, you shall descend from the dragon carriage or phoenix palanquin. Have Friar Sand remain at your side and help you mount the white horse. Old Monkey will then cast a body-fixing spell, leaving the queen, her ministers, and all their people unable to move, while we follow the main road straight west. After we have traveled for a full day and night, I shall recite a spell to release the enchantment, allowing the queen and her ministers to revive and return to the city. In this way, first, we shall not harm their lives, and second, your primal spirit will suffer no injury. This is the stratagem called ‘escaping the net by means of a false marriage.’ Does it not beautifully accomplish both ends at once?” On hearing this, Tripitaka was like a drunkard suddenly sobered, like a dreamer newly awakened. His joy dispelled his cares, and he thanked Pilgrim again and again, saying, “I am deeply grateful for my worthy disciple’s wise counsel.” The four travelers, united in heart and purpose, continued discussing their plan. We shall say no more of them for now.

Moreover, you have always been a benevolent and compassionate man who harms not even a single living soul upon the road. If countless innocent people were killed, how could your heart endure it? It would truly be an evil deed.”
After hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, your reasoning is excellent.
But I fear that once the queen summons me inside, she will demand the rites of husband and wife. How could I consent to lose my primal yang and ruin the virtue of the Buddhist order?
How could I spill my true essence and cast away the human body attained within our faith?”
Pilgrim said, “Once you consent to the marriage today, she will surely come out of the city with an imperial procession to receive you with the honors due an emperor.
Do not refuse her. Simply ride in her phoenix palanquin or dragon carriage, ascend the jeweled hall, and take your seat facing south.
Ask the queen to bring out the imperial seal, summon us brothers to court, stamp our travel rescript, and then have the queen write and sign an endorsement before handing it over to us.
Meanwhile, have a banquet prepared; it can serve at once to celebrate your union with the queen and to bid us farewell.
When the banquet is over, order the procession prepared again, saying that you will escort the three of us out of the city and return afterward to be joined with the queen.
Thus you will beguile the queen and her ministers into rejoicing, so that they harbor no thought of obstructing us and conceive no cruel or malicious intent.
Once they have escorted us beyond the city, you shall descend from the dragon carriage or phoenix palanquin. Have Friar Sand remain at your side and help you mount the white horse.
Old Monkey will then cast a body-fixing spell, leaving the queen, her ministers, and all their people unable to move, while we follow the main road straight west.
After we have traveled for a full day and night, I shall recite a spell to release the enchantment, allowing the queen and her ministers to revive and return to the city.
In this way, first, we shall not harm their lives, and second, your primal spirit will suffer no injury.
This is the stratagem called ‘escaping the net by means of a false marriage.’ Does it not beautifully accomplish both ends at once?”

On hearing this, Tripitaka was like a drunkard suddenly sobered, like a dreamer newly awakened. His joy dispelled his cares, and he thanked Pilgrim again and again, saying, “I am deeply grateful for my worthy disciple’s wise counsel.”
The four travelers, united in heart and purpose, continued discussing their plan. We shall say no more of them for now.

p.src: Now the Grand Preceptor and the posthouse mistress, without waiting to be summoned, went straight through the court gates to the white jade steps and reported, “Your Majesty’s auspicious dream has proved perfectly true. The joy of a union between fish and water is at hand.” At this report the Queen rolled up the pearl curtain, descended from the dragon bed, parted her cherry lips to reveal silver teeth, and asked with a radiant smile in her tender voice, “When you saw the Imperial Brother, my worthy minister, what did he say?” The Grand Preceptor said, “When we reached the posthouse and had paid our respects to the Imperial Brother, we explained the marriage proposal in full. The Imperial Brother still offered words of refusal, but fortunately his senior disciple readily consented, agreeing to leave his master here to become Your Majesty’s husband and reign as emperor, facing south. He asked only that their travel document first be exchanged and the three disciples sent on their way west; once they have obtained the scriptures and returned, they will come here to acknowledge their new father and mother and ask for travelling expenses back to Great Tang.” The Queen laughed. “And what else did the Imperial Brother say?” The Grand Preceptor reported, “The Imperial Brother said nothing, thereby consenting to become Your Majesty’s spouse. Only his second disciple insisted that he must first be given a banquet and wine.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Queen immediately issued an edict ordering the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a feast. At the same time she ordered the imperial procession prepared so that she might go outside the city to welcome her husband. All the women officials reverently obeyed the royal command, sweeping the palace halls and laying out the courtyards and terraces. One group hastened to arrange the banquet; another made the royal equipage ready with meteoric speed. Though the Kingdom of Western Liang was a land of women, the splendour of its imperial carriage was in no way inferior to that of China. This is what could be seen:

p.src: The Queen came forward, seized Tripitaka by the hand, and called in a sweet, coquettish voice, “Dear Imperial Brother, please mount the dragon carriage. Come with me to the Golden Throne Hall, and let us be joined as husband and wife.” The elder trembled so violently that he could scarcely stand, as though drunk or dazed. Wukong prompted him from the side, “Master, there is no need for such modesty. Please mount the carriage with our new mistress. Have our travel document exchanged quickly and let us go fetch the scriptures.” The elder dared not reply. He brushed Wukong aside twice, but could not stop his tears from falling. Wukong said, “Master, do not distress yourself. If you will not enjoy such wealth and honour as this, what are you waiting for?” Tripitaka had no alternative but to comply. Wiping away his tears, he forced a cheerful expression, stepped forward, and with the Queen:

p.src: When the civil and military officials saw their sovereign and the elder mount the phoenix carriage together and sit shoulder to shoulder, every one of them beamed with delight. They turned the ceremonial procession about and re-entered the city. Only then did the Great Sage Sun tell Sha Monk to shoulder the luggage and lead the white horse, and together they followed behind the royal procession. Zhu Bajie dashed wildly ahead, reached the Five Phoenix Tower first, and shouted, “How easy! Everything is ready-made for us! This will never do, never do at all! We must drink the wedding wine before the marriage is consummated.” The women officials bearing the ceremonial objects and leading the procession were so startled that they returned one after another to the royal carriage and reported, “Your Majesty, that long-snouted, big-eared fellow is shouting in front of the Five Phoenix Tower that he wants wedding wine.” On hearing the report, the Queen leaned her fragrant shoulder against the elder and nestled her peachlike cheek beside his. Opening her sandalwood-red lips, she asked coyly, “Dear Imperial Brother, which of your distinguished disciples is that long-snouted, big-eared one?” Tripitaka replied, “He is my second disciple. He was born with an enormous appetite and has spent his whole life pursuing rich food. Some wine and food must first be prepared for him to eat before anything else can be done.” The Queen asked urgently, “Has the Court of Imperial Entertainments finished preparing the feast?” A woman official reported, “It is ready. Both meat and vegetarian banquets have been laid out in the Eastern Pavilion.” The Queen asked again, “Why two kinds?” The woman official replied, “Your servant feared that the Imperial Brother of Tang and his distinguished disciples ordinarily eat vegetarian food, so both meat and vegetarian fare were prepared.” The Queen smiled sweetly, nestled against the elder’s fragrant cheek, and asked, “Dear Imperial Brother, do you eat meat or vegetarian food?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk eats vegetarian food, but I have never abstained from wine. We shall need a few cups of vegetarian wine for my second disciple and me.”

p.src: When they arrived below the Eastern Pavilion, they heard a lovely swell of pipes and song and saw two rows of charming, rosy-cheeked beauties. In the centre of the main hall two sumptuous banquets had been laid: the place of honour on the left held the vegetarian feast, and the place of honour on the right the meat feast. Below them, on either side, were all single places. The Queen gathered up her robe sleeves and, holding a jade cup in her ten slender fingers, came forward to conduct the guests to their seats. Wukong stepped forward and said, “My master and all his disciples are vegetarians. Please seat Master first at the vegetarian banquet on the left, then move the next three places down and divide them between the two sides so that we brothers may sit.” The Grand Preceptor said delightedly, “Quite right, quite right. Master and disciples are like father and sons; they must not sit shoulder to shoulder.” The women officials hurriedly rearranged the tables. The Queen personally offered each of the three disciples a cup and seated them. Wukong then gave the Tang Monk a wink, signalling his master to return the courtesy. Tripitaka came down, raised a jade cup in turn, and conducted the Queen to her seat. The civil and military officials bowed toward the throne and gave thanks for the imperial favour. Each sat on one side or the other according to rank; only then did the music cease and the wine begin to circulate.

p.src: Bajie cared nothing for manners or propriety. He gave his belly free rein and did nothing but eat. He paid no heed to what he was devouring—jade-grain rice, steamed buns, sugar cakes, mushrooms, fragrant shiitake, bamboo shoots, wood ear fungus, daylily buds, agar, laver, turnips, taro, radishes, yams, or Solomon’s seal—but gobbled the whole lot down until nothing remained. Then he drank five or seven cups of wine. He shouted, “Bring more food! Fetch a great goblet! Let us drink a few more big cups, then each of us can attend to his own business.” Sha Monk asked, “Why attend to any business when there is such a fine banquet to enjoy?” The fool laughed. “The ancients said, ‘Let the bowyer make bows and the fletcher make arrows.’ Now among us, whoever is taking a husband should take one, whoever is marrying should marry, whoever is fetching scriptures should go on fetching scriptures, and whoever has a road to travel should go on travelling. We must not keep craving wine and delay our business. Hurry up and issue our travel document. As the saying goes, the generals do not dismount; each hastens toward his own future.” When the Queen heard him, she immediately ordered that large cups be brought. The attendants hastily brought parrot cups, cormorant ladles, golden bowls, silver beakers, glass cups, crystal basins, Penglai bowls, and amber goblets. They filled them to the brim with jade liquor and poured an unbroken stream of exquisite wine, and sure enough everyone drank another round.

p.src: Tripitaka rose slightly from his seat, pressed his palms together before the Queen, and said, “Your Majesty, many thanks for this lavish feast. I have had enough wine. Please ascend to the throne hall, endorse our travel permit, and, while the day is still young, send the three of them out of the city.” The Queen did as he asked. Taking the elder with her, she ended the banquet and proceeded to the golden throne hall, where she invited him to take the throne at once. “No, no,” said Tripitaka. The Grand Preceptor said just now that the auspicious way of Heaven will open tomorrow; only then would this poor monk dare ascend the throne and assume the royal title. Today, let us merely stamp the travel permit and send them on their way.” The Queen complied. She resumed her seat upon the dragon throne, had a golden armchair placed to its left, and invited the Tang Monk to sit there. He told his disciples to bring forth the travel credential. The Great Sage had Sha Monk untie the luggage and take out the document. The Great Sage presented it in both hands. The Queen examined it closely. At the top were nine imperial seals of the Great Tang emperor, and below them the seals of the kingdoms of Baoxiang, Black Rooster, and Cart-Slow. After reading it, the Queen asked with a sweet, delicate laugh, “So my royal brother’s family name is also Chen?” Tripitaka replied, “My lay family name is Chen, and my Dharma name is Xuanzang. By the sacred grace of my Tang emperor, I was acknowledged as his royal brother and granted Tang as my surname.” The Queen asked, “Why are the names of your worthy disciples absent from the document?” Tripitaka replied, “My three unruly disciples are not subjects of the Tang realm.” The Queen asked, “If they are not men of your Tang realm, why were they willing to accompany you here?” Tripitaka said, “My eldest disciple is a native of the kingdom of Aolai in the Eastern Continent of Superior Body; the second is a native of Wusi Village in the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift; and the third is from the River of Flowing Sands. All three had transgressed the laws of Heaven, but the Bodhisattva Guanyin of the Southern Sea delivered them from their suffering. They embraced goodness and took refuge in the faith, resolving to atone for their crimes through merit, and willingly undertook to protect me on my journey west to fetch the scriptures. I took them all as disciples along the road, which is why their Dharma names were not entered in the document.” The Queen said, “Shall I add their Dharma names for you?” “As Your Majesty wishes,” replied Tripitaka. The Queen immediately ordered ink and brush to be brought. The fragrant ink was ground thick and the fragrant brush charged full; at the end of the document she wrote the names Sun Wukong, Zhu Wuneng, and Sha Wujing. Only then did she take out the royal seal and stamp it squarely upon the document; she also added her signature flourish. She had it passed down. The Great Sage Sun received it and told Sha Monk to wrap it securely away.

p.src: The Queen then bestowed a tray of small pieces of gold and silver. Stepping down from the dragon throne, she handed it to the Pilgrim and said, “You three may use this for traveling expenses and hasten westward; when you return with the scriptures, I shall reward you handsomely again.” The Pilgrim replied, “We who have left the household accept neither gold nor silver. There will be places along the road where we can beg for alms.” Seeing that he would not accept it, the Queen brought out ten bolts of fine damask and brocade and said to the Pilgrim, “As you are in such haste to depart, there is no time to have garments tailored. Take these and make clothes along the road to ward off the cold.” The Pilgrim replied, “Those who have left the household may not wear damask or brocade. We have cloth robes enough to protect us.” Seeing that he would not accept this either, the Queen ordered, “Bring three sheng of imperial rice, to provide them with at least one meal upon the road.” At the word “meal,” Eight Rules promptly accepted it and tucked it into the luggage. The Pilgrim said, “Brother, our luggage is heavy enough already. How is it that you still have the strength to carry rice?” Eight Rules laughed. “What do you know? Rice is the finest sort of perishable cargo. One meal is all it takes to settle the account.” Thereupon they pressed their palms together and thanked her for her grace.

p.src: Tripitaka said, “May I trouble Your Majesty to accompany this poor monk in seeing the three of them out of the city? Once I have given them a few instructions and told them to journey carefully westward, I shall return. Then, free of every care and attachment, I shall share everlasting glory with Your Majesty, and only then may phoenix and mate be joined in union.” The Queen, unaware that this was a ruse, ordered the royal procession prepared. Resting beside Tripitaka’s fragrant person, she mounted the phoenix carriage with him and set out through the western gate. Throughout the city, cups were filled with pure water and rare incense burned in the censers: the people came first to behold the Queen’s royal procession, and second to see the male form of her royal brother. Young and old alike were all women with powdered, lovely faces and glossy black hair piled in cloudlike coiffures. Before long, the royal procession left the city and reached a point beyond the western pass.

p.src: The Pilgrim, Eight Rules, and Sha Monk were of one mind. Having made themselves ready, they went straight to meet the royal carriage and cried out sternly, “There is no need for the Queen to escort us any farther. We shall take our leave here.” The elder slowly descended from the dragon carriage, bowed with clasped hands to the Queen, and said, “Your Majesty, please return. Allow this poor monk to go and fetch the scriptures.” At these words the Queen turned pale with shock. Seizing the Tang Monk, she said, “My royal brother! I offered you the wealth of an entire kingdom and asked you to become my husband. Tomorrow you were to ascend the exalted throne and reign as sovereign, while I became your queen. We have even partaken of the wedding feast—how can you change your mind now?” Hearing this, Eight Rules worked himself into a fury. Twisting his snout and flapping his ears wildly, he barged before the carriage and shouted, “What would monks like us want with marrying a painted skeleton like you? Let our master go on his way!” Seeing him rage and make such hideous faces, the Queen was frightened out of her wits and collapsed into the carriage. Sha Monk snatched Tripitaka out of the crowd and helped him mount his horse.

p.src: Just then a woman darted out from beside the road and shouted, “Royal Brother of Tang, where do you think you are going? Come away and make merry in love with me!” Sha Monk cursed, “Ignorant villain!” He drew his precious staff and struck straight at her head. The woman conjured up a whirlwind. With a whoosh, she swept the Tang Monk away, vanishing without a trace, and no one knew where she had taken him. Ah! Indeed:
